stimuli.title: A North African traveler's account of a West African court, 1350s (practice text)
stimuli.text: The king holds audience in a pavilion hung with silk, and his guards carry lances worked with gold. His judges studied the law in Fez and Cairo, and in the mosques of the town boys learn to recite the Quran in Arabic, though at home their fathers speak the tongue of the country. Caravans from the north unload slabs of salt and carry away gold dust, and the merchants praise the king's officers for keeping the roads free of thieves.

stimuli.title: A Chinese official's memorial to the emperor, 1100s (practice text)
stimuli.text: Since the new early-ripening rice was brought from the south, the fields of the river valleys give two harvests a year, and the markets of the capital overflow. Yet a full granary is not enough. The empire must be governed by men who have mastered the classics and passed the examinations, so that office goes to the learned and the virtuous, not to the sons of great families.

stimuli.title: A Persian court historian on the Mongol khans, c. 1300 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The khans have made the roads from China to the lands of the Franks safe for merchants. Post stations stand a day's ride apart, and a tablet from the khan opens every gate. Physicians from Cathay work beside our own, and astronomers from many lands meet in the observatory. Yet the cities that resisted them, Baghdad among them, were left in ruins.

stimuli.title: A historian's interpretation (practice text)
stimuli.text: By the 1200s the Abbasid caliphs held little power outside Baghdad. Real authority had passed to Turkic military rulers, the Seljuks and later others, who claimed to defend the faith while governing in their own name. Yet the decline of the caliphate did not end the intellectual life of Dar al-Islam. Scholars in Cairo, Damascus and Samarkand went on translating, studying and adding to Greek, Persian and Indian learning in medicine, mathematics and astronomy.

stimuli.title: An Arab merchant's description of a city on the East African coast, 1330s (practice text)
stimuli.text: The houses of the town are built of coral stone, and its sultan lives in a palace above the harbor. Ships arrive from Arabia, Persia and India when the winds of winter blow from the northeast and leave when they turn in summer. The people trade ivory and gold from the interior for cloth, beads and porcelain. They speak a language of their own, though many of its words are Arabic, and the merchants pray in the mosque on the shore.

stimuli.title: A Spanish soldier's memoir of a Mexica city, written in the 1560s about 1519 (practice text)
stimuli.text: From the hills we looked down on their capital, set on an island in the lake and linked to the shore by long causeways, with fields of mud and reeds built up out of the shallows around it. In the market thousands bought and sold maize, cotton cloth, cacao and feathers. Officials told us that every province subject to their lord sent tribute of food, cloth and captives, and that many of those provinces hated him for it.

stimuli.title: A Buddhist monk's account of a visit to a Southeast Asian kingdom, 1290s (practice text)
stimuli.text: The great temple of the capital was built by earlier kings for the Hindu gods, and its walls are carved with the stories of Vishnu. Today most of the people follow the teaching of the Buddha, and monks in yellow robes walk the streets each morning. Water from the reservoirs flows through canals to the rice fields, and the king's officers watch over it closely.

stimuli.title: A historian's interpretation (practice text)
stimuli.text: The plague that struck Afro-Eurasia in the 1340s traveled the same roads and sea lanes that carried silk and spices. In places it killed a third or more of the people. In western Europe the survivors found their labor suddenly scarce, and many peasants demanded and won higher wages or left their lords for the towns. In the Islamic world and China the losses were as great, but the social results differed from place to place.

stimuli.title: A Spanish chronicler's description of the Inca state, 1550s (practice text)
stimuli.text: The lords of Cuzco joined their lands with roads that climb the mountains and cross the gorges on bridges of rope. Every household owed the state a turn of labor each year, building roads, working the lord's fields or serving as soldiers. Officials kept the accounts of every province on knotted cords, which they read as well as we read our books.

stimuli.title: A European ambassador's letter from the Ottoman court, 1550s (practice text)
stimuli.text: The sultan's governors are not great lords with lands of their own but his servants. His officers take boys from the Christian villages of the Balkans, raise them as Muslims and train them for the palace or the army, and the ablest rise to govern provinces. His foot soldiers carry firearms and are drilled every day, and his cannon brought down the walls of cities we thought could never fall. In Istanbul the great mosques rise over the city to proclaim his glory.

stimuli.title: Selected land-based empires, c. 1450 to c. 1750
stimuli.text:
| Empire | Ruling group | Religion of the rulers | Most subjects |
|---|---|---|---|
| Ottoman | Turkic dynasty | Sunni Islam | Muslims, with large Christian and Jewish minorities |
| Safavid | Turkic-Persian dynasty | Shia Islam | Muslims in Persia |
| Mughal | Central Asian Turkic-Mongol dynasty | Sunni Islam | Hindus |
| Qing | Manchus from the northeast | Buddhism and Confucian state rites | Han Chinese |

stimuli.title: A Mughal court historian's account of the emperor's debates, 1580s (practice text)
stimuli.text: On Thursday nights the emperor gathers learned men of every faith in the hall of worship: Sunni and Shia scholars, Brahmins, Jain teachers, Zoroastrian priests and even the Jesuit fathers from Goa. He listens to them argue and asks questions of his own. He has lifted the tax that non-Muslims paid, and Rajput princes who follow the Hindu gods command his armies and sit in his council.

stimuli.title: Two historians' interpretations (practice text)
stimuli.text:
**Historian A:** The Ottoman, Safavid and Mughal states owed their rise to firearms. Cannon broke the walls of rival cities, and infantry with muskets defeated the horse archers who had ruled the battlefield for centuries. Only rulers rich enough to buy guns and pay soldiers could compete, and so power gathered in a few large states.

**Historian B:** Guns were available to many rulers; what set the great empires apart was how they governed. They built salaried bureaucracies, surveyed land for taxes, bargained with local elites and religious leaders, and used splendid courts and buildings to persuade subjects that their rule was just.

stimuli.title: A Persian shah's proclamation, early 1500s (practice text)
stimuli.text: Let it be known in every city of our realm that the faith of the Twelve Imams is the faith of this kingdom. Preachers shall honor the family of the Prophet in every Friday sermon, and scholars of that faith are invited from Arabia and Lebanon to teach in our cities. Those who curse the Imams shall be punished, and the enemy to the west who denies them shall find us ready.

stimuli.title: A German pamphlet, 1520s (practice text)
stimuli.text: The Christian is saved by faith alone, not by buying pardons from Rome. Every man may read the Scriptures for himself, now that the printers have put them into our own tongue for a few coins. Why should German princes send their silver south to build churches in Rome, when the Pope has no power over the conscience that God has not given him?

stimuli.title: A scholar's chronicle of a West African empire, 1650s (practice text)
stimuli.text: In the days of the great askia the empire reached from the ocean to the lands east of the river. Timbuktu was full of scholars who taught law and grammar in the mosques, and students came to them from across the Sahel. Then the army of the sultan of Morocco crossed the desert with muskets and cannon, which our cavalry had never faced, and the empire broke apart.

stimuli.title: A Portuguese captain's report to his king, 1510s (practice text)
stimuli.text: We found these seas full of ships, Arab, Gujarati and Chinese, trading in pepper, cloth and spices as their fathers did. They have no fleet that can stand against our guns. We have taken the port of Goa and built a fortress there, and no ship may now sail these waters without a pass from our captains. Those that refuse are seized, and the duties we collect will pay for the fleet many times over.

stimuli.title: A Chinese scholar's essay on silver, 1630s (practice text)
stimuli.text: Silver now pours into our ports from the ships of the foreigners at Luzon, who bring it across the great ocean from their mines in lands far to the east. The court demands that the land tax be paid in silver, so the farmer must sell his grain for coin. When the ships fail to come, silver grows dear, and the farmer must sell twice as much grain to pay the same tax.

stimuli.title: Estimated number of enslaved Africans carried across the Atlantic, by period (rounded)
stimuli.text:
| Period | Enslaved Africans embarked |
|---|---|
| 1501-1600 | 0.3 million |
| 1601-1700 | 1.9 million |
| 1701-1800 | 6.5 million |
| 1801-1866 | 3.9 million |

Note: estimates of people put on ships in Africa. Many died during the voyage.

stimuli.title: Orders from a Japanese shogun's council to the governor of a port, 1640s (practice text)
stimuli.text: The Portuguese ships are not to be received again; their priests stirred up the peasants of the south to rebellion, and every household in the domains must now show each year, at its Buddhist temple, that it holds no part in their teaching. Our own people are not to cross the sea, and none who has gone abroad is to be let back. The Dutch, who bring no priests, may keep their trading house on the small island in the harbor, and Chinese junks may still come, both under the watch of the governor.

stimuli.title: A historian's interpretation (practice text)
stimuli.text: The crops that crossed the oceans after 1500 changed diets far from the Americas. Maize and cassava became staple foods across much of West and Central Africa, and sweet potatoes and maize could be grown on Chinese hillsides where rice would not grow. In the other direction, sugar cane, carried from the Old World to the Caribbean and Brazil, became the crop around which whole colonial societies were built.

stimuli.title: A Dutch merchant's report to the directors of his company, 1620s (practice text)
stimuli.text: The company now holds the islands where the nutmeg grows, and no other nation may buy a single nut except from us. We have built our headquarters at Batavia, where the ships gather before the voyage home. The shareholders in Amsterdam may expect a handsome return, for we fix the price of spices in Europe as we please.

stimuli.title: A planter's letter from a Caribbean sugar island, 1730s (practice text)
stimuli.text: We must buy new Africans every year, for the work of the cane fields and the boiling houses wears them out faster than children are born to replace them. Some run off to the mountains, where the free communities of runaways take them in. These people have beaten our soldiers more than once, and the governor now talks of a treaty with them.

stimuli.title: Two historians' interpretations (practice text)
stimuli.text:
**Historian A:** The revolution in Saint-Domingue began in Paris. When the French revolutionaries declared that men are born free and equal in rights, they handed the enslaved people of the richest colony in the world a language of liberty that they turned against their masters, and against France itself.

**Historian B:** The enslaved of Saint-Domingue needed no French pamphlets to know that slavery was wrong. Most were born in Africa, many had been soldiers there, and the colony's sugar estates worked them to death. Their rising in 1791 grew from that experience, from African traditions and from networks built among the plantations.

stimuli.title: A Japanese reformer's essay, 1870s (practice text)
stimuli.text: When the black ships came into our harbor, we learned that courage and swords are no match for steam and cannon. If Japan is not to be carved up like China, we must learn from the West what makes it strong. The government has sent students to Europe and America, built railways and mills, and raised an army of conscripts. Let us take their science and their industry, and keep our own spirit.

stimuli.title: A speech to a town council in New Granada by a locally born lawyer, 1810 (practice text)
stimuli.text: Gentlemen, our families have lived on this soil for generations, yet the judges, the bishops and the viceroy all come to us from across the sea. Our merchants may sell only to Cadiz, at the prices Cadiz sets. Now the king is a prisoner of the French emperor, and the junta that claims to rule in his name was never chosen by us. Let this council form a government of its own, as the English colonies of the north did, for a people has the right to choose who governs it.

stimuli.title: A British factory inspector's report, 1840s (practice text)
stimuli.text: In the cotton mills of this district I found children of nine and ten tending the machines beside women who work twelve hours a day, with little air and less light. The owners say the mills cannot pay without them, and the parents need their wages. The town has doubled in twenty years; whole families crowd into cellars, and the river that turns the mill wheels also carries away the sewage.

stimuli.title: A provincial lawyer's pamphlet, published in Paris, 1789 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The commons plough the fields, keep the shops and pay the taille, while the lords and the abbots, who pay almost nothing, take the commands in the army and the seats in the high courts as if they were born to them. Why should the deputies of twenty million count for no more than those of a few hundred thousand? Authority comes from the nation, not from the crown, and the law must be made by those whom the nation elects.

stimuli.title: A speech by a German nationalist, 1848 (practice text)
stimuli.text: We speak one language, sing the same songs and share a thousand years of history, yet we are divided into dozens of states, each with its own prince and its own customs border. Let the Germans become one nation with one parliament, chosen by the people and bound by a constitution, and no foreign power will dare to treat us as a battlefield again.

stimuli.title: A British antislavery society's pamphlet, 1820s (practice text)
stimuli.text: Parliament ended the trade in human beings in 1807; it must now end slavery itself in the West Indies. Every spoonful of sugar on a British table is sweetened with the sweat of the enslaved. Let every family that loves justice refuse slave-grown sugar, and let every town send its petition to Westminster.

stimuli.title: A British colonial official's report on India, 1880s (practice text)
stimuli.text: The railways now carry raw cotton from the interior to Bombay in days rather than weeks, and it leaves for the mills of Lancashire, which send back cloth cheaper than any village weaver can make. Since the rising of the sepoys, the Crown governs directly, and order is everywhere kept. Yet the educated Indians who staff our offices have begun to meet in congresses of their own and to ask why they may not govern their own country.

stimuli.title: A contract for a laborer leaving India for a Caribbean colony, 1870s (practice text)
stimuli.text: The laborer agrees to work on any estate in the colony to which he is sent, for five years, nine hours a day, at the wage fixed by the government. He shall receive housing and medical care. At the end of ten years in the colony he may claim a free passage home, or he may take a grant of land and remain.

stimuli.title: A Chinese governor's letter to a foreign ruler, 1839 (practice text)
stimuli.text: A good ruler watches over his people as a father over his sons, and he would not wish the sons of another house to be harmed by his servants. Yet the smugglers who sail under your flag bring chests of the black drug to our coast, and for it our silver leaves the empire year after year while our soldiers and clerks lie idle in the smoking dens. By the emperor's order every chest in the port has been taken and destroyed. Lawful trade in tea and silk may go on; the drug may not.

stimuli.title: A West African ruler's reply to a European officer, 1890s (practice text)
stimuli.text: Your officer says that I must sign his paper and fly his flag, but my fathers ruled this land before his people knew it existed. Your nations met in a city far away and divided our lands among themselves without asking a single king of Africa. If you come with your guns, I will fight you, though I know that your rifles fire faster than ours.

stimuli.title: A New Zealand settler's letter home, 1860s (practice text)
stimuli.text: The government means to have the land of the Waikato, treaty or no treaty, for the settlers keep coming and every ship brings more. The Maori chiefs say they never sold it and will not sell, and they have built forts that our soldiers find hard to take. But they cannot hold out for ever against the numbers and the guns that are coming.

stimuli.title: A letter from a Chinese laborer in Southeast Asia to his family, 1880s (practice text)
stimuli.text: I am working in the tin mines of Malaya, where the pay is three times what I could earn at home, though the work is hard and fever is common. The broker took most of my first year's wages to pay for my passage. Send word of Mother. If the harvest fails again, my brother should come here too; many men from our village are already in this town.

stimuli.title: A British investor's report on Argentina, 1890s (practice text)
stimuli.text: British capital has built the railways that run from the pampas to Buenos Aires, and British ships carry the wheat and frozen meat to our markets. The estancia owners grow rich, and Argentina buys our rails, locomotives and cloth in return. A young country could not hope for better partners.

stimuli.title: A soldier's letter from the Western Front, 1915 (practice text)
stimuli.text: We have held this same mile of mud since the winter. The guns never stop, and when we go over the top the machine guns cut us down before we reach the wire. Beside us are men from India, and further down the line the French have brought regiments from Senegal. At home, they say, women run the munitions factories and every family buys war bonds.

stimuli.title: A speech by an Indian nationalist leader, 1940s (practice text)
stimuli.text: Britain asks us to fight for freedom in Europe while she denies it to us at home. We will not be drawn into this war without the promise of our independence. Our weapon is not the sword but the refusal to cooperate: we will not obey unjust laws, we will not buy foreign cloth, and we will fill the jails until the government cannot rule.

stimuli.title: A historian's interpretation (practice text)
stimuli.text: By the 1980s the Soviet economy could no longer pay for both an arms race and the promises of socialism. Reforms meant to save the system, more openness and a loosening of central planning, instead let its critics speak. When the states of Eastern Europe threw off their communist governments in 1989, Moscow did not send the tanks, and within two years the Soviet Union itself was gone. Its end opened much of the world to market economies and freer trade.

stimuli.title: World population, selected years (rounded estimates)
stimuli.text:
| Year | World population |
|---|---|
| 1900 | about 1.6 billion |
| 1950 | about 2.5 billion |
| 2000 | about 6.1 billion |

stimuli.title: A historian's interpretation (practice text)
stimuli.text: The crash of 1929 spread from Wall Street to the world because so many economies were tied to American loans and to the sale of raw materials whose prices collapsed. Unemployment soared in Germany, and farmers in Latin America and Africa saw their incomes fall by half. Many people lost faith in liberal democracy and in free markets, and movements on the far right promised work, order and national glory.

stimuli.title: A Chinese villager's memoir of land reform, written in the 1980s (practice text)
stimuli.text: When the Japanese left, the war between the parties came to our county. In 1950 the cadres arrived, called the village together and read out the landlords' names. The land was measured and divided, and for the first time my father farmed fields of his own. A few years later we were told to join the collectives, and then came the years of the great campaign, when the steel furnaces burned and the fields went untended.

stimuli.title: A statement by a South African student group, 1980s (practice text)
stimuli.text: Our parents were moved from their homes under laws that reserve the best land for whites. We must carry passes to work in our own country, and we are taught in separate schools to be servants. While the rest of Africa has won its freedom, we are still ruled by a minority. We call on the world to stop trading with this government until all South Africans vote.

stimuli.title: A factory manager's interview in a Southeast Asian export zone, 1990s (practice text)
stimuli.text: Our plant sews sports shoes for a company whose offices are in another continent. The designs arrive by computer, and the finished shoes leave in steel containers on ships that call here each week. Most of our workers are young women from the villages. The wages are low by foreign standards but higher than farm work, and when protests abroad complained of our conditions, the company sent inspectors.

stimuli.title: A historian's interpretation (practice text)
stimuli.text: The Ottoman Empire entered the First World War in 1914 and did not survive it. Arab leaders who rose against the sultan expected independence, but the victors divided the Arab provinces between Britain and France as mandates under the League of Nations. In Anatolia, nationalist officers drove out occupying armies and founded a Turkish republic that abolished the sultanate and set out to build a secular state.

stimuli.title: A Japanese government pamphlet, 1940 (practice text)
stimuli.text: Asia must be freed from the Western powers that have exploited it for a century. Under Japan's leadership the peoples of East Asia will build a sphere of common prosperity, where the oil, rubber and tin of the south and the industry of Japan work together. Those who resist this new order resist the liberation of Asia itself.

stimuli.title: A speech at a conference of Asian and African states, 1955 (practice text)
stimuli.text: We who meet here have known colonial rule, and most of us have only just won our freedom. We will not exchange one master for another. We are told that we must join one camp or the other in the struggle between the great powers. We refuse. Our task is to feed our people and build our nations, and to speak for peace.

stimuli.title: A public health officer's report, 1980 (practice text)
stimuli.text: The last natural case of smallpox was found three years ago, and the disease that killed hundreds of millions is now gone from the earth. It was defeated by vaccine teams sent to every country, by searches from village to village, and by governments on both sides of the Cold War working together. We must now turn the same methods against other diseases.

questions.stem: The court described in the account most directly built its wealth on
options: control of trade across the Sahara
spices shipped across the Indian Ocean
taxes on pilgrims sailing to Mecca by sea
silver mined by forced native labor
questions.explanation: Mali's rulers taxed and protected the trans-Saharan trade in which northern merchants exchanged salt for West African gold. Silver mining and the spice trade belong to other regions.

questions.stem: The mosques and Arabic learning described in the account were mainly a result of
options: missionary work by Christian orders
a Mongol policy of religious conversion
the conquest of the region by the Abbasid army
the spread of Islam along trade routes
questions.explanation: Muslim merchants carried Islam across the Sahara, and West African rulers and elites adopted it, which also eased trade with North Africa. The Abbasids never conquered the region.

questions.stem: Which state of the same period was most similar to the one described, in the source of its wealth?
options: The Swahili city-states of East Africa
The Kamakura shogunate in Japan
The Inca state in the Andes
The Holy Roman Empire in central Europe
questions.explanation: Like Mali, the Swahili city-states grew rich by controlling long-distance trade, in their case across the Indian Ocean. The Inca relied on labor tribute and had no market trade of this kind.

questions.stem: The traveler's point of view is best explained by the fact that he
options: was a European merchant hoping to trade for gold directly
was a Muslim visitor who judged the court partly by its faith
had never traveled outside North Africa before making this one visit
was a West African official writing to praise his own ruler
questions.explanation: A North African traveler shared the faith of Mali's elite, so he noticed its judges, mosques and Quran schools and the safety of merchants. He was a visitor, not a court official.

questions.stem: The two harvests described in the memorial most directly led to
options: a sharp decline in commerce in Chinese cities
rapid population growth in Song China
a shift from rice to wheat in southern China
the end of the examination system
questions.explanation: Fast-ripening rice from Champa (in Southeast Asia) allowed more harvests, which fed a fast-growing population and busy commercial cities. The examination system continued.

questions.stem: The official's view of how the empire should be governed most directly reflects
options: the Mongol practice of giving office to foreigners
Buddhist teaching that officials should withdraw from the world
Neo-Confucian ideas about merit and learning
Legalist demands for harsh punishment of all officials
questions.explanation: The memorial ties office to mastery of the classics and to virtue, the Confucian ideal behind the civil service examinations that Song rulers expanded. Mongol rule came later.

questions.stem: Which of the following best describes a continuity in China after the period of the memorial?
options: Later dynasties gave up rice for other grains
Later dynasties kept a bureaucracy chosen by examinations
Later dynasties gave the highest offices only to Buddhist monks
Later dynasties ended all trade with foreign merchants
questions.explanation: The Ming and Qing kept the examination system and its scholar-officials until 1905, apart from a pause under the Mongols. Rice farming and foreign trade continued too.

questions.stem: The conditions on the roads described by the historian most directly encouraged
options: the closing of the Silk Roads to foreign merchants
the end of contact between China and Persia
greater trade and exchange of ideas across Eurasia
the decline of the Indian Ocean trade network
questions.explanation: Under the Mongols, protected roads and relay stations made long-distance travel safer, and goods, scholars and techniques moved between China, Persia and Europe. The routes were open, not closed.

questions.stem: The ruin of Baghdad mentioned in the account refers to
options: the Mongol conquest that ended the Abbasid caliphate
the Crusaders' capture of the city
an Ottoman siege that ended a thousand years of Byzantine rule
the Black Death's arrival in Iraq
questions.explanation: Mongol armies sacked Baghdad in 1258 and killed the last Abbasid caliph there. Crusaders never took Baghdad, and the Ottoman siege that ended Byzantine rule was at Constantinople.

questions.stem: The connections described in the account also help explain
options: the rapid spread of the plague in the 1340s
the rise of the Atlantic slave trade
the decline of paper making in Europe
the arrival of the first Portuguese ships in India
questions.explanation: The same routes that carried merchants across the Mongol lands carried the plague from Central Asia to the Mediterranean in the 1340s. The Atlantic slave trade and the Portuguese came later.

questions.stem: The practice of taking boys from Christian villages described in the letter is known as
options: the mit'a
the encomienda
the hacienda
the devshirme
questions.explanation: Under the devshirme, the Ottomans took Christian boys from the Balkans, converted them and trained them as janissary soldiers or officials loyal only to the sultan. The other systems were in the Americas.

questions.stem: The sultan's purpose in the practice the ambassador describes was most likely to
options: reduce the size of his standing army
create officials and soldiers loyal only to him
spread Christianity within the palace
give more power to the old Turkish noble families
questions.explanation: Officials and soldiers raised in the palace owed everything to the sultan, not to a noble family, which helped him control a large empire. The practice weakened, not strengthened, the old nobility.

questions.stem: The ambassador's comments on firearms and cannon best illustrate
options: the Ottoman refusal to adopt European technology
the spread of steam power to the eastern Mediterranean
the use of gunpowder weapons to expand land empires
the decline of Ottoman military power by the 1550s
questions.explanation: Ottoman cannon and musket-armed infantry helped conquer Constantinople, the Balkans and much of the Middle East. Steam power came three centuries later.

questions.stem: The great mosques mentioned in the letter served the same purpose as which of the following?
options: Missions that Spanish priests built on the edges of their empire
Trading posts that European companies built on the coasts of India
Fortified towns that peasants built to defend themselves from their lords
Monumental buildings that other rulers used to display their legitimacy
questions.explanation: Rulers such as the Mughals and the Qing used grand buildings to show power and divine favor, as the Ottomans did with their mosques. Trading posts and missions had other purposes.

questions.stem: Which conflict is most directly explained by the information in the Ottoman and Safavid rows of the table?
options: Wars between the Qing and the Ottoman sultans
Wars between the Ottomans and the Safavids
Wars between the Safavids and the Spanish
Wars between the Mughals and the Qing
questions.explanation: The Sunni Ottomans and the Shia Safavids fought for over a century, a rivalry shaped by religious difference as well as by borders and trade. The Mughals and Qing never fought a major war.

questions.stem: The table suggests that the Mughal and Qing empires faced a similar challenge, namely
options: governing a small island population
replacing the old languages of their own ruling dynasties
ruling a large majority that differed from the ruling group
defending a single faith against Christian invaders
questions.explanation: Muslim Mughal rulers governed a mostly Hindu population, and Manchu Qing rulers governed a far larger Han Chinese majority. Both had to win the cooperation of local elites.

questions.stem: Which policy did the Qing use to address the challenge shown in the last row of the table?
options: Moving the capital to Manchuria
Keeping the Confucian examinations and Han officials
Banning all Han Chinese from every government post
Converting all subjects to Shia Islam
questions.explanation: The Qing kept the Confucian examination system and employed many Han officials alongside Manchus, while also requiring the queue hairstyle as a sign of loyalty. They ruled from Beijing.

questions.stem: A historian arguing that these empires tolerated diversity in order to rule could best use which evidence?
options: The Ottomans took boys from Christian villages
Ottoman millets let religious communities run their own affairs
The Safavids made Shia Islam the official faith of the whole state
The Qing made men wear the queue
questions.explanation: The Ottoman millet system let Christian and Jewish communities keep their own laws and leaders under the sultan. The other examples show rulers imposing uniformity or control.

questions.stem: The captain's report best illustrates the Portuguese effort to
options: convert the Mughal emperors to Christianity
end trade between Gujarat and China
settle large farming colonies in India
control Indian Ocean trade by force at sea
questions.explanation: The Portuguese did not build a large territorial empire in Asia; they seized ports such as Goa and forced ships to buy passes, taxing trade they could not otherwise dominate.

questions.stem: The captain's description of ships already trading in the region shows that
options: Chinese merchants had stopped sailing by 1500
the Indian Ocean had no trade before the Portuguese came
Europeans entered a trade network that already existed
Europeans brought spices to Asia for the first time
questions.explanation: Gujarati, Arab, Persian and Chinese merchants had traded across the Indian Ocean for centuries; the Portuguese joined and tried to tax that network rather than creating it.

questions.stem: Which development made the voyages described in the report possible?
options: New ships and navigation tools such as the caravel
The invention of the steamship
Mongol maps of the Atlantic
The opening of a canal across Egypt linking the Mediterranean and the Red Sea
questions.explanation: Portuguese sailors used ships such as the caravel and tools such as the astrolabe and better maps, some of them learned from Islamic and Chinese sources, to reach Asia around Africa.

questions.stem: The Portuguese approach described in the report differed most from Spanish rule in the Americas in that the Portuguese in Asia
options: relied on forced native labor in silver mines
converted most of the local population to Christianity by force
settled large numbers of European farmers
held fortified ports instead of large inland territories
questions.explanation: In Asia the Portuguese built a trading-post empire of fortified ports, while the Spanish conquered large populations and lands in the Americas and used forced labor in mines.

questions.stem: The silver described in the essay came mainly from
options: gold fields in West Africa
mines in Japan, carried by Dutch ships through Nagasaki
mines in Spanish America, carried by way of Manila
mines in England
questions.explanation: Silver from Potosi and Mexico crossed the Pacific on the Manila galleons, and Spanish traders in the Philippines (Luzon) exchanged it for Chinese silk and porcelain.

questions.stem: Which Chinese policy most directly increased demand for the silver described in the essay?
options: A tax on imports of silk
The printing of paper money in every province
A requirement that taxes be paid in silver
A ban on all foreign trade
questions.explanation: Ming reforms in the late 1500s, often called the Single Whip, combined taxes and required them in silver, so China drew in silver from Japan and the Americas.

questions.stem: The scholar's complaint about falling supplies of silver best illustrates
options: China's refusal to trade with Europeans
the rising value of grain in China compared with silver
the end of the Manila galleon trade across the Pacific in the 1630s
how global trade could cause hardship far from its source
questions.explanation: When fewer silver ships arrived, silver grew dear and farmers had to sell more grain to pay taxes, showing how the Pacific silver trade tied Chinese farmers to events across the ocean.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best support Historian A's argument?
options: Accounts of secret meetings among enslaved people on estates
Reports of very high death rates on sugar plantations
Rebel leaders quoting the Declaration of the Rights of Man
Records showing that most enslaved people were born in Africa
questions.explanation: Historian A traces the revolution to French revolutionary ideas, so leaders using the language of the Declaration of the Rights of Man would support that view. The other choices fit Historian B.

questions.stem: Historian B would most likely emphasize which cause of the revolution?
options: British efforts to seize the colony
Spanish support for the rebels
Debates in the French National Assembly about rights
The experience of the enslaved themselves
questions.explanation: Historian B points to the enslaved people's African backgrounds, the brutality of the sugar estates and networks among plantations, not French debates.

questions.stem: The revolution discussed by the historians resulted in
options: British rule over Saint-Domingue
the restoration of slavery in Saint-Domingue
the first state founded by formerly enslaved people
a constitutional monarchy ruled from Paris by the French king
questions.explanation: The rebellion ended slavery in the colony and, after defeating French forces, created independent Haiti in 1804, the first state founded by people who had freed themselves from slavery.

questions.stem: Both historians would agree that the revolution in Saint-Domingue
options: was led mainly by wealthy European settlers and merchants
had no link to events in France
failed to end slavery in the colony
belonged to a wider age of Atlantic revolutions
questions.explanation: Historian A links it to the French Revolution and Historian B to conditions in the colony, but both treat it as a revolution of the same era. Both note it was led by the enslaved.

questions.stem: The black ships mentioned in the essay refer to
options: a British fleet that conquered Kyoto and deposed the emperor
the American warships that pressed Japan to open its ports
Chinese warships sent to invade Japan
Dutch merchant ships trading at Nagasaki
questions.explanation: In 1853 and 1854 American warships under Commodore Perry forced the Tokugawa shogunate to open ports to trade, a shock that helped bring down the shogunate.

questions.stem: The reforms described in the essay are best described as
options: a rejection of all Western technology
a return to rule by the shogun
state-sponsored industrialization
a policy of closing Japan to trade
questions.explanation: After the Meiji Restoration of 1868, the government built railways and factories, sent students abroad and created a conscript army to strengthen Japan.

questions.stem: The reforms in the essay were most similar to which other effort of the 1800s?
options: The Ottoman Tanzimat reforms
The British Factory Acts
The Qing ban on opium
The Russian conquest of Central Asia
questions.explanation: The Tanzimat reforms also tried to strengthen an Asian state against the West by modernizing law, the army and education. The Factory Acts regulated labor in an already industrial country.

questions.stem: The program described in the essay most directly made it possible for Japan to
options: build an empire of its own in East Asia
abolish its army
end its trade with Western states
avoid all wars with its neighbors until the 1940s
questions.explanation: Industrial and military strength let Japan defeat China in 1895, taking Taiwan, and Russia in 1905, and then annex Korea in 1910.

questions.stem: The trade described in the report best illustrates
options: a British ban on all cotton exports from India to Europe
colonies supplying raw materials to industrial Britain
British demand for Indian finished cloth
Indian factories outproducing those of Britain
questions.explanation: Industrial Britain drew raw cotton from India and sold factory cloth back, a pattern of economic imperialism that hurt India's handloom weavers.

questions.stem: The rising of the sepoys mentioned in the report most directly led to
options: Mughal rule over all of India
direct rule of India by the British Crown
the end of British rule in India
the founding of the British East India Company
questions.explanation: After the revolt of 1857, Parliament ended the East India Company's rule and the Crown governed India directly through a viceroy.

questions.stem: The congresses described at the end of the report are an early sign of
options: British socialism
the Mughal revival
the partition of India
Indian nationalism
questions.explanation: Western-educated Indians founded the Indian National Congress in 1885, which grew into the main nationalist movement. Partition came only in 1947.

questions.stem: The economic relationship in the report was most similar to that between Britain and
options: Egypt, which grew cotton for British mills
Japan after 1900, which built its own industry
the United States after 1900, which exported machines
Germany, which built its own factories
questions.explanation: Egypt also exported raw cotton and imported manufactured goods under growing British control. Germany, Japan and the United States industrialized themselves.

questions.stem: The contract is an example of
options: the mit'a
serfdom
chattel slavery for life
indentured labor
questions.explanation: Indentured workers signed contracts for a fixed term of labor in return for passage, wages and sometimes land, unlike slaves, who were property for life.

questions.stem: Contracts like this one became common in the Caribbean mainly because
options: the slave trade to the Caribbean grew in the 1870s
European workers refused to leave the Caribbean islands
planters needed new workers after slavery was abolished
India had a shortage of workers
questions.explanation: After Britain abolished slavery, planters in Trinidad, Guyana and elsewhere recruited indentured workers from India and China to replace the labor of the formerly enslaved.

questions.stem: A lasting result of migrations like the one described in the contract was
options: the end of Hinduism in the Caribbean
the spread of the Inca language
large South Asian communities overseas
the return of every laborer to India after five years
questions.explanation: Many indentured workers stayed, and Trinidad, Guyana, Fiji, Mauritius and South Africa still have large communities of South Asian descent.

questions.stem: The conditions on the battlefield described in the letter were most directly caused by
options: machine guns and heavy artillery
the use of cavalry charges as the main tactic
the lack of railways to carry men and shells near the front
a shortage of soldiers on both sides
questions.explanation: Machine guns, artillery and barbed wire favored defenders, producing years of trench warfare on the Western Front. Railways brought men and shells to the front.

questions.stem: The soldier's description of life at home best illustrates
options: a return to peacetime production during the war
a government refusal to borrow any money to pay for the war
the end of women's paid work in Europe
total war, in which whole societies were mobilized
questions.explanation: In total war, states directed economies, sold war bonds, used propaganda and drew women into factory work to supply the front.

questions.stem: The presence of soldiers from India and Senegal in the letter is best explained by
options: a German policy of recruiting colonial soldiers
European powers drawing on their colonies for troops
India and Senegal declaring war on Germany as independent states
the League of Nations sending peacekeepers
questions.explanation: Britain and France recruited over a million colonial soldiers for the war; India and Senegal were colonies, not independent states.

questions.stem: Colonial service in the war described in the letter most directly contributed to
options: the end of the British Empire in 1919
growing demands for self-rule after 1918
the immediate independence of all French colonies in Africa
a decline of nationalism in Asia
questions.explanation: Colonial subjects who served expected reward, and broken promises after 1918 strengthened nationalist movements in India, Africa and elsewhere.

questions.stem: The war referred to in the speech also weakened Britain by
options: ending its alliance with the United States
making it the world's largest creditor
giving it new colonies in Asia
draining its money and military strength
questions.explanation: The Second World War left Britain deep in debt and exhausted, which made holding India and other colonies far harder.

questions.stem: The methods the speaker proposes are best described as
options: a military coup
armed guerrilla warfare
a request for a League of Nations mandate
nonviolent civil disobedience
questions.explanation: Refusing to obey unjust laws, boycotting foreign cloth and filling the jails are methods of nonviolent noncooperation used by the Indian National Congress.

questions.stem: Independence for British India in 1947 also brought
options: a single state with one religion
rule by the Mughal family restored
union with Burma and Ceylon as one large federal state
partition into India and Pakistan
questions.explanation: The British divided India into Hindu-majority India and Muslim-majority Pakistan; millions fled across the new borders and hundreds of thousands died.

questions.stem: The path to independence in the speech differed most from that of Algeria, which
options: won independence after a long armed war
became independent from France before the Second World War began
won independence peacefully with no conflict
never sought independence from France
questions.explanation: Algeria, with a large French settler population, won independence in 1962 after an eight-year war. India's movement relied mainly on mass nonviolent protest.

questions.stem: According to the historian, the Soviet Union collapsed partly because
options: it adopted free trade with the West in the 1950s and grew too fast
Eastern Europe invaded it in 1989
its economy could not pay for the arms race
it won the arms race too quickly
questions.explanation: The historian points to an economy strained by military spending and failing to deliver, and to reforms that let critics speak.

questions.stem: Which other communist state of the 1980s chose economic reform while keeping the party's political control?
options: Czechoslovakia
Poland
East Germany
China
questions.explanation: China opened its economy to markets and foreign investment from 1978 but kept one-party rule. Poland, East Germany and Czechoslovakia ended communist rule in 1989.

questions.stem: The historian's last sentence best describes which development of the 1990s?
options: A return to closed national economies
The end of trade between western Europe and Russia
The expansion of Soviet power into Asia
The spread of market economies and global trade
questions.explanation: After the Cold War, former communist states moved to markets and many joined global trade bodies, part of the wider globalization of the 1990s.

questions.stem: Which organization, founded in 1995, set rules for the freer trade the historian mentions?
options: The Warsaw Pact
The World Trade Organization
The Organization of Petroleum Exporting Countries
The League of Nations
questions.explanation: The World Trade Organization replaced the earlier GATT in 1995 and set rules for trade among its members; Russia and China later joined. OPEC is a group of oil-exporting states.

questions.stem: Which development most directly helped make possible the change in the table between 1950 and 2000?
options: The end of international trade in grain
Rising death rates from infectious disease in most regions
A fall in the world's food supply
New seeds and farming methods
questions.explanation: The Green Revolution's high-yield seeds, fertilizers and irrigation raised food output, while vaccines and antibiotics cut death rates, so population grew fast.

questions.stem: The trend in the table most directly contributed to
options: a fall in carbon emissions
greater strain on water and forests
a shrinking demand for energy
the end of urban growth in most countries after 1950
questions.explanation: More people using more resources increased pressure on water, forests and the atmosphere, and fossil fuel use and emissions rose.

questions.stem: Which change in medicine most directly contributed to the trend in the table?
options: The spread of bloodletting
The decline of public health spending
Antibiotics and mass vaccination
The invention of the printing press
questions.explanation: Antibiotics and vaccines, spread widely after 1945, sharply reduced deaths from infectious disease, especially among children.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best support the historian's claim about intellectual life?
options: Translations of Greek works into Arabic used by later scholars
A rise in the price of paper in Baghdad
A decree by the caliph closing the libraries of Cairo and Cordoba
The conversion of the Seljuk rulers to Buddhism
questions.explanation: The historian argues learning continued despite political decline; Arabic translations and commentaries on Greek works, later used in Europe, show that. A decree closing libraries would undercut it.

questions.stem: The historian's description of Turkic military rulers best illustrates
options: new states arising as the caliphate lost power
the unification of the Islamic world under one ruler
the replacement of Islam by Turkic religions
the conquest of Persia by Christian kingdoms
questions.explanation: As the Abbasid caliphate weakened, Turkic groups such as the Seljuks built their own states in its lands while keeping and defending Islam. The Islamic world grew more divided, not less.

questions.stem: The learning described by the historian most directly affected Europe through
options: the spread of Buddhism along the Silk Roads
the decline of trade across the Mediterranean Sea after 1200
the transmission of texts by way of Spain and Sicily
the conquest of Rome by Seljuk armies
questions.explanation: Scholars in Muslim Spain and Sicily translated Arabic works and Arabic versions of Greek texts into Latin, feeding learning in European universities. No Seljuk army reached Rome.

questions.stem: The timing of the ships' arrivals and departures described in the account depended on
options: the steam engines used by Arab ships
the opening of the Suez Canal
the monsoon winds of the Indian Ocean
the Mongol relay stations on land routes
questions.explanation: Indian Ocean sailors timed voyages to the seasonal monsoon winds, which blow from the northeast in winter and from the southwest in summer. Steam and the Suez Canal came centuries later.

questions.stem: The language described in the account is best explained by
options: the migration of Turkic peoples into Africa
Portuguese rule over the coastal towns
the permanent settlement of the whole coast by Chinese sailors
contact between Bantu-speaking Africans and Arab traders
questions.explanation: Swahili is a Bantu language that took in many Arabic words through centuries of trade with Arab and Persian merchants. Portuguese rule came only after 1500.

questions.stem: Compared with the trans-Saharan trade, the trade described in the account differed mainly in that it
options: did not involve any Muslim merchants at all
was controlled entirely by the Mongols
traded mostly in enslaved Europeans
moved goods by sea rather than by caravan
questions.explanation: Both trades brought Muslim merchants and African gold into contact, but the East African trade moved by ship across the Indian Ocean while the Saharan trade moved by camel caravan.

questions.stem: In the early 1400s, which state sent large fleets that reached ports on this coast?
options: The Ottoman Empire
The Inca Empire
The Mughal Empire
Ming China
questions.explanation: Ming China sent Zheng He's treasure fleets across the Indian Ocean between 1405 and 1433, and some reached East Africa. The Mughal Empire did not exist until 1526.

questions.stem: The tribute described in the memoir shows that the Mexica state
options: drew wealth from conquered peoples it ruled
had no markets or merchants
relied mainly on trade with Europe
was a small state with no subject provinces
questions.explanation: The Mexica built an empire by conquering neighbors and demanding tribute of goods and captives. The memoir describes a large market, and contact with Europe began only in 1519.

questions.stem: The Mexica system described in the memoir was most similar to the Inca system in that both states
options: had no religious role for the ruler
used iron weapons and horses in war
relied on markets as their main source of revenue
demanded goods or labor from subject peoples
questions.explanation: Both states drew on subject peoples: the Mexica through tribute and the Inca through the mit'a labor system. Neither had iron tools or horses before contact.

questions.stem: The resentment of subject provinces mentioned in the memoir helps explain
options: why some native peoples allied with the Spanish
why the Spanish failed to conquer the city
why the Mexica abandoned the city before 1519
why the Spanish brought no allies on their march
questions.explanation: Peoples such as the Tlaxcalans, enemies of the Mexica, joined the Spanish, and their warriors were vital in the fall of the city in 1521. The Spanish did conquer the city.

questions.stem: The emperor's policies described in the account most directly reflect
options: a plan to expel the Portuguese from India
religious tolerance used to win the loyalty of subjects
the influence of Confucian scholars on Mughal rule
an effort to make Sunni Islam the only faith in the empire
questions.explanation: Akbar debated with scholars of many faiths, ended the jizya on non-Muslims and gave Hindu Rajput princes high posts, binding a diverse empire to his rule.

questions.stem: Which later development marked a change from the policies described in the account?
options: A later emperor brought back the tax on non-Muslims
Later emperors ended the use of Persian at the imperial court
Later emperors converted to Christianity
Later emperors gave up all lands south of Delhi
questions.explanation: Aurangzeb restored the jizya in 1679 and favored stricter Sunni practice, which angered Hindu subjects and helped fuel revolts such as the Maratha rising.

questions.stem: The fact that the account was written by a court historian suggests that it
options: records the views of ordinary villagers
was written to criticize the emperor's religion
presents the emperor in a favorable light
was meant for Jesuit readers in Europe
questions.explanation: A historian employed at court wrote for the emperor and his circle, so the account is likely to praise him. It tells us about court life more than about villagers.

questions.stem: The presence of Jesuit fathers from Goa in the account is best explained by
options: a British colony already ruling all of India by the 1580s
the Mughal conquest of Portugal
Portuguese trading posts and missions on the Indian coast
the Jesuits' control of the Silk Roads
questions.explanation: The Portuguese held Goa from 1510 as a trading base, and Jesuit missionaries traveled from there to the Mughal court. British rule over most of India came much later.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best support the argument of Historian A?
options: Ottoman rulers granting religious communities their own self-rule
Safavid shahs building a splendid capital at Isfahan
Ottoman cannon breaching the walls of Constantinople in 1453
Mughal land surveys used to set tax rates
questions.explanation: Historian A credits firearms; the cannon that broke the walls of Constantinople fit that view. Land surveys, buildings and self-rule fit Historian B's focus on governing.

questions.stem: Which evidence would best support Historian B's argument?
options: The use of horse archers by Central Asian rivals
A battle won by musket-armed infantry
Mughal officers paid salaries based on rank
The price of cannon in the 1500s
questions.explanation: Akbar's mansabdar system paid officers by rank and tied them to the state, the kind of administration Historian B stresses. The other choices concern weapons.

questions.stem: The two historians would most likely agree that
options: guns played no role in Ottoman conquests
large land-based empires grew stronger
bureaucracy mattered far more than firearms in every case
the empires collapsed by 1500
questions.explanation: Both explain the rise of strong empires; they differ on the cause. Historian A would reject the claim that bureaucracy mattered more, and Historian B does not deny that guns existed.

questions.stem: Historian B's argument could also be applied to which state outside the Islamic world?
options: The Dutch Republic, with its trading companies
Qing China, with its examination-based officials
The Swahili city-states, with their merchant councils
The Iroquois Confederacy, with its alliances of nations
questions.explanation: The Qing ruled through a large, trained bureaucracy and Confucian legitimacy, the methods Historian B stresses. The Iroquois and Swahili cities were not large bureaucratic empires.

questions.stem: Which development most directly explains the rise shown in the table between 1601 and 1800?
options: The decline of the Mughal Empire in northern India
The end of slavery in the British Empire
The spread of sugar plantations in the Americas
Spanish conquest of the Philippines
questions.explanation: Sugar plantations in Brazil and the Caribbean, which killed workers quickly and needed ever more labor, drove the growth of the Atlantic slave trade.

questions.stem: The smaller total in the last row of the table is best explained by
options: the European conquest of Africa's interior
the end of plantation farming in both Brazil and Cuba
bans on the slave trade by Britain and other states
a sharp drop in world demand for sugar
questions.explanation: Britain banned its slave trade in 1807 and its navy patrolled against others, and other states followed. Brazil and Cuba still bought captives until 1850 and the 1860s, so the trade shrank but did not end at once; the last row also covers only 66 years.

questions.stem: The trend in the table most directly contributed to which change in West Africa?
options: The spread of Christianity across the Sahel
Fewer men than women in some regions
The rise of large cities based on manufacturing
The decline of every African state
questions.explanation: Slave traders took more men than women, leaving some West African regions with fewer working-age men. Some states, such as Dahomey and Asante, grew more powerful in the trade.

questions.stem: Which piece of evidence would best support the note under the table?
options: Census counts of free people in Europe
Prices of sugar in London
Records of deaths on board slave ships
Lists of African rulers who traded with Europeans
questions.explanation: The note says many people died on the voyage; ship records of deaths during the Middle Passage would show it. Sugar prices and rulers' names say nothing about deaths at sea.

questions.stem: The orders best illustrate the Tokugawa shogunate's effort to
options: expand Japanese trade and settlement across the Pacific
end all contact with China
limit foreign influence while keeping some trade
convert Japan to Christianity
questions.explanation: Tokugawa rulers banned Christianity and travel abroad but let the Dutch, and Chinese merchants, trade under control at Nagasaki. Japan did not cut all contact.

questions.stem: The council's measures against the foreign priests' teaching were most likely a response to
options: fears that Christian converts would be disloyal
a Spanish invasion of Kyoto
Dutch missionaries preaching in the Japanese countryside
the spread of Buddhism from Korea
questions.explanation: The shogunate saw Christian converts, and the Spanish and Portuguese missionaries behind them, as a threat to its control, especially after the Shimabara revolt of 1637 and 1638, in which many rebels were Christian. The Dutch did not preach.

questions.stem: The policy in the orders was most similar to which policy of the same era?
options: Spanish encouragement of foreign settlers in Mexico
Chinese limits on where Europeans could trade
Mughal welcome of Jesuit missionaries at court
Ottoman grants of trading rights to all Europeans
questions.explanation: Ming and later Qing rulers also controlled foreign trade, eventually confining Europeans to Canton. The Mughal court welcomed Jesuits, which is the opposite of the orders.

questions.stem: The speaker most likely belonged to which group?
options: Creoles, of European descent but born in the Americas
Enslaved Africans on sugar estates
Peninsulares, officials born in Spain
Indigenous nobles descended from the rulers of the Inca state
questions.explanation: Creole elites resented being kept from high office and from free trade by Spanish-born peninsulares, and they led most of the Spanish American independence movements.

questions.stem: According to the speech, which event gave the colonies the chance to break with Spain?
options: The Mexican-American War
Napoleon's seizure of the Spanish throne
Britain's ban on the Atlantic slave trade in 1807
The British victory in the Seven Years' War
questions.explanation: When Napoleon made his brother king of Spain in 1808, colonial elites refused to obey the new government, and many juntas moved toward independence.

questions.stem: The right the speaker claims shows the influence of
options: the divine right of kings
Confucian ideas of order
mercantilist economic theory and colonial trade rules
Enlightenment ideas of popular sovereignty
questions.explanation: The speaker appeals to the right of a people to choose who governs it, an Enlightenment idea also used in the American and French revolutions.

questions.stem: After independence, most of the new states of Spanish America
options: kept much of the old social order in place
became colonies of the United States
ended the Catholic Church's role in society
gave the land of large estates to indigenous farmers across the region
questions.explanation: Independence ended Spanish rule but left large estates, the church and creole elites in place, and many indigenous and mixed-race people saw little change.

questions.stem: The conditions in the report were a direct result of
options: the Industrial Revolution in Britain
the enclosure of land by the Mughals
the Black Death
the British conquest of China
questions.explanation: Factory production of cotton cloth, powered first by water and then by steam, drew families into crowded mill towns in Britain in the late 1700s and 1800s.

questions.stem: The inspector's remark that the town has doubled in twenty years best illustrates
options: rapid urbanization as people moved to factory work
the decline of the cotton industry in northern England
the spread of guild workshops in the countryside
a movement of families from industrial towns back to farms
questions.explanation: Factory jobs drew rural families into mill towns such as Manchester, which grew faster than housing, water and sewers could keep up with. Cotton was Britain's leading industry.

questions.stem: Reports like this one most directly led to
options: the British move to free trade with China and India
the end of the factory system in Britain
the abolition of the British monarchy
laws limiting child labor and working hours
questions.explanation: Inspectors' reports helped persuade Parliament to pass Factory Acts that limited children's work and hours. The factory system kept growing.

questions.stem: Which thinker responded to conditions like those in the report by arguing that workers should own the means of production?
options: Karl Marx
Confucius
Adam Smith
John Locke
questions.explanation: Marx and Engels argued that industrial capitalism exploited workers and predicted that workers would take over the means of production. Smith defended free markets.

questions.stem: The official's complaint about silver refers to
options: a trade imbalance caused by British opium sales
a shortage of silver in Britain
China's purchase of British cotton cloth
the arrival of silver in China from Spanish America
questions.explanation: Before opium, Britain paid silver for Chinese tea; once British merchants sold opium from India, silver flowed out of China instead.

questions.stem: The seizure of opium described in the letter most directly led to
options: the end of tea exports from China
a ban on opium in every European country and colony
a Chinese conquest of British India
a war that forced China to sign unequal treaties
questions.explanation: Britain went to war, and the Treaty of Nanjing of 1842 opened ports, ceded Hong Kong and began a series of unequal treaties.

questions.stem: Which internal challenge also weakened the Qing in the decades after the letter?
options: The Glorious Revolution
The Taiping Rebellion
The Meiji Restoration
The Sepoy Rebellion
questions.explanation: The Taiping Rebellion of 1850 to 1864 killed millions and nearly toppled the dynasty. The Meiji Restoration was in Japan, the Sepoy Rebellion in India and the Glorious Revolution in England.

questions.stem: The official's argument would be most persuasive to readers who
options: believed free trade must never be limited by any government
lived in the British colony of India
wanted to expand the opium trade
believed a ruler must protect the health of subjects
questions.explanation: The letter appeals to a ruler's duty to protect his people, and asks the foreign ruler to apply the same duty to the harm his own subjects do in China.

questions.stem: The meeting in a city far away mentioned in the reply refers to
options: the Berlin Conference of 1884 and 1885
the Treaty of Tordesillas
the Congress of Vienna of 1815
the Paris Peace Conference that followed the war of 1914
questions.explanation: European powers met in Berlin in 1884 and 1885 to set rules for claiming African territory, without any African rulers present.

questions.stem: The ruler's comment about rifles points to which factor in the European conquest of Africa?
options: The warm welcome Europeans received from most African rulers
Advantages in weapons such as repeating rifles and machine guns
A shortage of horses in Europe
The end of the slave trade in 1700
questions.explanation: Breech-loading and repeating rifles and the Maxim gun gave European armies a large edge, and quinine let them survive malaria in the interior.

questions.stem: Which African state successfully resisted European conquest in this period?
options: Egypt, which drove out the British
The Congo, which expelled the Belgians
Ethiopia, which defeated Italy at Adwa
The Zulu kingdom, which kept its independence
questions.explanation: Ethiopia used modern rifles and artillery to defeat an Italian army at Adwa in 1896 and stayed independent. The Zulu kingdom was conquered by Britain in 1879.

questions.stem: According to the historian, the crash spread worldwide mainly because
options: every country used the same currency
all countries had abandoned farming
the League of Nations ordered banks in every country to close
economies were linked by loans and trade
questions.explanation: The historian ties the crisis to American loans and collapsing commodity prices, which carried the depression to Europe, Latin America and Africa.

questions.stem: The historian's last sentence best explains
options: the rise of fascist movements in the 1930s
the decline of nationalism in Germany
the end of the Soviet five-year plans for heavy industry
the spread of democracy across Europe
questions.explanation: Mass unemployment helped parties such as the Nazis in Germany win support with promises of work, order and national revival.

questions.stem: Unlike the economies the historian describes, the Soviet Union in the 1930s
options: relied on free markets and foreign loans
used state planning and forced industrialization
had no heavy industry at all
was hit hardest of all by the stock market crash of 1929
questions.explanation: Stalin's five-year plans and collectivization built heavy industry under state control, at great human cost, largely apart from world markets.

questions.stem: Which response to the crisis in the historian's account differed from the fascist response?
options: Expanding territory by war to gain land and resources
Building a cult around a single leader
Banning all political parties but one
Democracies expanding the state's role in the economy
questions.explanation: Democracies such as the United States and Sweden used public works and welfare programs within democratic systems; the other choices describe fascist and militarist states.

questions.stem: The war between the parties mentioned in the memoir was fought between
options: the Communists and the Nationalists
China and the Soviet Union over the border
the Qing and the Taiping
China and India
questions.explanation: After Japan's defeat in 1945, the Chinese Civil War resumed between Mao Zedong's Communists and the Nationalists, ending in a Communist victory in 1949.

questions.stem: The land reform described in the memoir is best described as
options: the redistribution of landlords' land to peasants
the sale of public land to foreign companies and banks
the return of land to Qing nobles
a plan to replace farming with mining
questions.explanation: The Communists took land from landlords, often after public accusation meetings, and gave it to poor peasants.

questions.stem: The great campaign described at the end of the memoir led to
options: a severe famine
the end of communist rule
a rapid rise in grain production
China joining NATO
questions.explanation: During the Great Leap Forward, starting in 1958, farmers were pulled into backyard steel making and unrealistic quotas, and the famine that followed killed tens of millions.

questions.stem: The move from land reform to collectives in the memoir was most similar to
options: Mexico's growth of large haciendas in the 1800s
Japan's land tax of the 1870s
the British enclosure of common land
Soviet collectivization of farms in the 1930s
questions.explanation: Like Soviet collectivization, Chinese collectives put private farms under state-directed group control, and both were followed by famine.

questions.stem: The laws described in the statement were part of
options: the Bantustans' independence from South Africa
apartheid, a system of legal racial segregation
the mandate system of the League of Nations
Britain's indirect rule through local chiefs and kings
questions.explanation: Apartheid, enacted from 1948, classified people by race, controlled movement with passes and kept Black South Africans from the vote.

questions.stem: The statement's reference to the rest of Africa winning its freedom refers to
options: the end of the Cold War
the Berlin Conference of 1884
the independence of many African colonies
the abolition of the Atlantic slave trade in the 1800s
questions.explanation: From Ghana in 1957, most of Africa won independence in the next two decades, leaving white-minority rule in South Africa increasingly isolated.

questions.stem: The call for the world to stop trading with the government contributed to
options: international sanctions on South Africa
South Africa's conquest of its neighbors
a sharp rise in foreign investment in South African mines
the end of all trade in Africa
questions.explanation: Boycotts, divestment campaigns and government sanctions in the 1980s raised the cost of apartheid and helped push the government to negotiate.

questions.stem: What change followed the campaign described in the statement?
options: Rule by a British governor again
A white-only republic that lasted until 2010
A ban on all political parties
Elections open to all races in 1994
questions.explanation: Negotiations ended apartheid, and in 1994 South Africans of all races voted in the first fully democratic election.

questions.stem: The factory described in the interview best illustrates
options: a colony producing raw materials for Europe
a craft workshop selling only to local markets in its own region
companies moving production to lower-wage countries
a state-owned factory in a planned economy
questions.explanation: Companies based in wealthy countries contracted factories in Asia and elsewhere where wages were lower, a key feature of economic globalization.

questions.stem: Which technologies mentioned in the interview made this kind of production possible?
options: Railways and steam looms
Radio and airships
Computers and container shipping
Telegraph cables and sailing ships
questions.explanation: Computer networks sent designs instantly, and standard steel containers cut the cost of moving goods by sea.

questions.stem: The manager's remark about protests abroad is best used as evidence of
options: the end of factory work in Asia
global campaigns over working conditions
government bans on all exports of shoes and clothing
falling demand for sports shoes
questions.explanation: Campaigns by students, unions and consumers in the 1990s pressed brands over sweatshop conditions, part of a broader reaction to globalization.

questions.stem: The account best illustrates which development in Southeast Asia?
options: The end of rice farming in the region
The influence of Hindu and Buddhist traditions from South Asia
The spread of Confucian civil service examinations to every kingdom
The arrival of Christianity through Portuguese missions
questions.explanation: Southeast Asian states such as the Khmer adopted Hindu and Buddhist ideas carried from South Asia by traders and monks, and the great temple changed from Hindu to Buddhist use. Portuguese missions came after 1500.

questions.stem: The reservoirs and canals described in the account show that the kingdom's power rested partly on
options: trade in camels across the desert
a navy that ruled the Atlantic
control of water for rice farming
silver mines worked by enslaved people
questions.explanation: Khmer rulers organized reservoirs and canals that watered rice fields, and the food they produced supported the capital. The other choices describe other places and periods.

questions.stem: Unlike the kingdom described in the account, the Srivijaya state of the same region drew its power mainly from
options: silver from mines in the Americas
irrigated wheat farming in the river valleys of the interior
conquest of the Mongol Empire
control of sea trade through the Strait of Malacca
questions.explanation: Srivijaya, based on Sumatra, grew rich by controlling and taxing the sea lanes between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea. Land-based Khmer power rested on irrigated rice.

questions.stem: Which later change in maritime Southeast Asia came mainly through merchants?
options: The adoption of Shinto by the Javanese kings and their courts
The spread of Christianity to Angkor
The spread of Islam to ports such as Malacca
The conquest of Sumatra by the Inca
questions.explanation: From the 1300s and 1400s, Muslim traders carried Islam to ports such as Malacca, and many coastal rulers converted. Christianity arrived later with the Portuguese and Spanish.

questions.stem: According to the historian, the plague spread mainly by way of
options: trade routes across land and sea
Mongol attacks on Japan
Crusader armies returning from the east
pilgrims crossing the Atlantic
questions.explanation: The historian ties the plague to the roads and sea lanes that carried silk and spices: the trade networks linking Central Asia, the Mediterranean and Europe.

questions.stem: The historian's point about peasants in western Europe is best supported by evidence that
options: laborers won higher pay after the plague
towns emptied as peasants returned to the manors
serfdom grew stronger in western Europe
lords raised the labor dues owed by every peasant
questions.explanation: With fewer workers, laborers could demand more, and wages rose in many places; serfdom weakened in western Europe over the following century, despite lords' efforts to hold wages down.

questions.stem: Which statement would the historian most likely agree with?
options: The plague began in the Americas and spread east across the Atlantic
The plague was a shared crisis with different local effects
The plague had no effect on trade networks
The plague affected only western Europe
questions.explanation: The historian says the losses in the Islamic world and China were as great as in Europe but that social results differed from place to place.

questions.stem: The speed of the plague's spread in the 1340s is best explained by
options: the use of railways for long trips
the trade links the Mongol empires had fostered
the opening of new sea routes between Europe and the Americas
the closing of Mediterranean ports
questions.explanation: Mongol rule had tied Central Asia, China, Persia and the Black Sea ports together, and the plague moved along those links to the Mediterranean. Railways and the Americas came later.

questions.stem: The yearly turn of labor described in the account is known as
options: the encomienda
the mit'a
the jizya
the iqta
questions.explanation: The Inca mit'a required households to give labor to the state for set periods. The encomienda was a Spanish grant, the jizya a tax on non-Muslims, and the iqta a land grant in Islamic states.

questions.stem: The knotted cords described in the account were used to
options: decorate the temples of the sun
keep records for the state
measure the height of the mountains
send messages across the ocean
questions.explanation: The Inca kept census, tribute and other records on quipu, knotted cords read by trained officials. The Inca had no writing system of the European kind.

questions.stem: The Inca state described in the account differed from the Mexica state mainly in that the Inca
options: relied more on labor service and a road network
had no army and no subject peoples
were ruled by a council of wealthy merchants from the coast
collected all taxes in coined money
questions.explanation: Both ruled subject peoples, but the Inca built a centralized state held together by roads and the mit'a labor system, while the Mexica relied more on tribute from conquered city-states.

questions.stem: Feudal Japan and feudal Europe in the 1200s were similar in that both
options: relied on warriors who owed loyalty and service to lords
were united under a single emperor who held real power
were ruled by strong central bureaucracies chosen by exams
had no landed aristocracy
questions.explanation: Samurai served daimyo and the shogun, and knights served lords in Europe, in exchange for land or support. Real power in Japan lay with the shogun, not the emperor.

questions.stem: The Delhi Sultanate in South Asia is best described as
options: a Muslim state ruling over a mostly Hindu population
a Buddhist kingdom founded by monks
a Hindu empire that expelled all Muslims from northern India
a colony of the Song dynasty
questions.explanation: Turkic Muslim rulers founded the Delhi Sultanate in the early 1200s and ruled much of northern India, where most people were Hindu. Their rule saw both conflict and cultural blending.

questions.stem: The Bhakti movement in South Asia is best described as
options: a Muslim law school that enforced the jizya
a Buddhist revival led and funded by the Delhi sultans
a Hindu movement of personal devotion to a god
a movement to expel merchants from Indian ports
