questions.explanation: Bhakti poets and teachers urged personal devotion to a god, often in local languages, and some challenged caste rules. It grew alongside Sufi Islam in the same period.

questions.stem: The faith that the proclamation makes official is
options: Sikhism
Sunni Islam
Zoroastrianism
Shia Islam
questions.explanation: The faith of the Twelve Imams is Twelver Shia Islam, which Shah Ismail made the religion of the Safavid state in the early 1500s.

questions.stem: The enemy to the west mentioned in the proclamation was most likely
options: the Qing dynasty
the Sunni Ottoman Empire
the Portuguese in the Persian Gulf
the Mughal Empire
questions.explanation: The Ottomans lay west of Safavid Persia, followed Sunni Islam and fought the Safavids from the Battle of Chaldiran in 1514 onward. The Mughals lay to the east.

questions.stem: The shah's policy in the proclamation most likely aimed to
options: build a shared identity that set his state apart from its rivals
weaken the authority of the shah over the religious scholars of Persia
encourage subjects to convert to Christianity
end conflict with all neighboring states
questions.explanation: Making Shia Islam the state faith gave the Safavid realm a distinct identity and unity against its Sunni neighbors. It sharpened, rather than ended, conflict with them.

questions.stem: Which outcome of the policy in the proclamation has lasted into the present?
options: Iran remains a mainly Shia country
Persia gave up Islam for Buddhism
Iran became mainly Sunni after 1600
The Ottoman Empire became mainly Shia
questions.explanation: Safavid rule made Persia, today Iran, a largely Shia land, which it remains. The Ottoman lands stayed mostly Sunni.

questions.stem: The ideas in the pamphlet are most closely tied to
options: the Scientific Revolution in Europe
the Enlightenment
the Crusades
the Protestant Reformation
questions.explanation: Salvation by faith alone, reading Scripture in one's own language and rejecting the sale of indulgences were central Protestant ideas from the 1520s.

questions.stem: The pamphlet suggests that the new ideas spread quickly mainly because of
options: the Silk Roads
the telegraph
the printing press
the steam engine and railways
questions.explanation: The pamphlet notes that printers had put the Bible into German for a few coins. The movable-type printing press made cheap books and pamphlets possible from the mid-1400s.

questions.stem: The writer's appeal to German princes is best explained by
options: the princes' wish to lead and join the Catholic Reformation in Rome
the princes' plan to move the Pope to Germany
Ottoman control of the German states
rulers' interest in gaining power at the expense of the Church
questions.explanation: Many princes backed the Reformation partly because breaking with Rome let them keep church wealth and power for themselves. The Catholic Reformation was Rome's response.

questions.stem: A major result of the movement described in the pamphlet was
options: a century of religious wars in Europe
the conversion of the Ottoman sultans
the union of all German states in 1530
the immediate end of the Catholic Church
questions.explanation: Conflicts between Catholic and Protestant rulers led to wars such as the French Wars of Religion and the Thirty Years' War. The Catholic Church survived and reformed itself.

questions.stem: The empire described in the chronicle is
options: Songhai
Great Zimbabwe
Kongo
Ethiopia
questions.explanation: Songhai, ruled by the askias, controlled the middle Niger and the trade city of Timbuktu until a Moroccan army defeated it in 1591.

questions.stem: According to the chronicle, the empire fell mainly because of
options: a revolt by Portuguese settlers on the coast
the drying up of the Niger River
a plague that emptied Timbuktu
an invading army with gunpowder weapons
questions.explanation: The chronicle credits Morocco's muskets and cannon, which Songhai cavalry had never faced. The Moroccan victory at Tondibi in 1591 broke the empire.

questions.stem: The chronicle's description of Timbuktu shows continuity with an earlier period in that the city
options: remained a center of Islamic learning and trade
had become a Christian bishopric
had become the capital of the Portuguese in Africa
had stopped trading across the Sahara
questions.explanation: Timbuktu had been a center of Islamic scholarship and trans-Saharan trade under Mali, and it stayed one under Songhai.

questions.stem: Qing rulers required Han Chinese men to wear the queue hairstyle in order to
options: show their submission to Manchu rule
mark them as Buddhist monks
follow an old Ming custom
set officials apart from the merchant class
questions.explanation: The queue was a Manchu style, and requiring it was a public sign of loyalty to the new dynasty. Refusing it could be punished as rebellion.

questions.stem: The Ottoman conquest of Constantinople in 1453 most directly
options: opened the Atlantic slave trade
ended the Byzantine Empire
began the Protestant Reformation
ended the Safavid dynasty
questions.explanation: Mehmed II's capture of Constantinople ended the Byzantine Empire, and the city became the Ottoman capital, Istanbul.

questions.stem: In the Mughal Empire, zamindars were
options: local landholders who collected taxes for the state
Muslim judges who ruled on family law
slave soldiers raised in the palace
Portuguese merchants with trading rights in Mughal ports
questions.explanation: Zamindars collected land revenue from peasants and passed part of it to the state, keeping a share. Under British rule many became landlords.

questions.stem: According to the historian, crops from the Americas most directly led to
options: the end of rice farming in China
the spread of wheat to the Caribbean
a fall in sugar production in Brazil
new staple foods in Africa and China
questions.explanation: Maize, cassava and sweet potatoes became staples in Africa and China, often grown on land unsuited to older crops. Sugar production in Brazil grew.

questions.stem: The new crops described by the historian most likely contributed to
options: the collapse of the Qing dynasty in 1700
a decline in trade between China and Southeast Asia
population growth in China in the 1700s
famine in China in the 1700s
questions.explanation: Hardy American crops let farmers use hills and poor soil, helping China's population grow rapidly under the Qing in the 1700s.

questions.stem: The historian's last sentence refers to societies built around
options: silver mines in Japan
small family farms in Europe
fur trading posts in Canada and the Great Lakes
plantations worked by enslaved Africans
questions.explanation: Sugar cane needed heavy labor; in the Caribbean and Brazil it was grown on plantations worked mainly by enslaved Africans.

questions.stem: The movement of plants, animals and diseases that the historian describes is called
options: the Silk Roads
the Columbian Exchange
the Commercial Revolution
the Green Revolution
questions.explanation: The Columbian Exchange is the transfer of crops, animals, people and diseases between the hemispheres after 1492. The Green Revolution was a 1900s farming change.

questions.stem: The company described in the report is an example of
options: a joint-stock company
a Mongol trading partnership
a craft guild
a state-run mine
questions.explanation: The Dutch East India Company sold shares to investors who shared the risks and profits of long voyages, the joint-stock model also used by the English East India Company.

questions.stem: The merchant's claim that the company could fix the price of spices rested on
options: the ban on spices in Europe
control of the Silk Roads
a treaty signed with the Mughal emperor in Delhi
its monopoly over the islands that grew them
questions.explanation: By seizing the Banda Islands, the only source of nutmeg, the company could control supply and set prices in Europe.

questions.stem: The Dutch company described in the report was most similar to which other organization?
options: The Ottoman janissary corps
The Jesuit order
The Hanseatic League of the 1300s
The English East India Company
questions.explanation: The English East India Company was also a chartered joint-stock company with its own ships, forts and soldiers. The janissaries and Jesuits were not trading companies.

questions.stem: The intended audience of the report helps explain why the merchant stresses
options: the profits the shareholders can expect
the history of the spice trade before 1500
the religious beliefs of local rulers
the suffering of the people of the islands
questions.explanation: The report is written to the company's directors, who answered to shareholders, so it emphasizes control of supply and expected returns.

questions.stem: The planter's letter suggests that sugar plantations in the Caribbean
options: had death rates so high that planters relied on new imports
grew their workforce mainly through births
depended on Native American labor by the 1730s
used mostly European indentured workers rather than Africans by the 1730s
questions.explanation: Brutal work in the cane fields and boiling houses killed enslaved people faster than births replaced them, so planters kept buying new captives from Africa.

questions.stem: The free communities of runaways described in the letter are known as
options: encomiendas
missions
trading factories
maroon communities
questions.explanation: Maroons were people who escaped slavery and built free communities in mountains and forests, as in Jamaica, Suriname and Brazil.

questions.stem: The planter's mention of a treaty is best used as evidence that
options: most enslaved people on the island had won their freedom by the 1730s
resistance could force colonial governments to negotiate
planters welcomed the runaways' communities
colonial governments had no soldiers in the Caribbean
questions.explanation: Jamaican maroons fought British troops to a standstill and won treaties in 1739, showing that resistance could force concessions. Most enslaved people remained enslaved.

questions.stem: The Treaty of Tordesillas of 1494
options: created the Dutch East India Company
ended the Hundred Years' War
divided newly found lands between Spain and Portugal
opened all of China to European trade and missionaries
questions.explanation: The treaty drew a line in the Atlantic: Spain claimed lands to the west and Portugal to the east, which is why Brazil became Portuguese.

questions.stem: Mercantilism held that a state grew strong by
options: sharing colonial profits equally with the colonies that produced them
letting markets operate free of state rules
exporting more than it imported and drawing raw materials from colonies
abolishing all tariffs between nations
questions.explanation: Mercantilists believed wealth was limited, so states sought trade surpluses, stores of gold and silver, and colonies that supplied raw materials and bought finished goods.

questions.stem: Queen Nzinga of Ndongo and Matamba is best known for
options: leading the Haitian Revolution
building the first Dutch fort on the coast of Angola
resisting Portuguese expansion in West Central Africa
uniting Mali and Songhai
questions.explanation: In the 1600s Nzinga used war, diplomacy and alliances, including with the Dutch, to resist Portuguese slave-raiding and conquest in what is now Angola.

questions.stem: The pamphlet's argument reflects which development in France in 1789?
options: Noble demands for higher taxes on their own estates
Demands by the third estate for political power
Support for the absolute power of the king
Calls for a Catholic crusade
questions.explanation: Members of the third estate, the commoners, demanded a say in government equal to their numbers and formed the National Assembly in 1789.

questions.stem: The idea that the nation, not the king, is sovereign came mainly from
options: the Mongol law code
Enlightenment thinkers
Confucian scholars
the Catholic Reformation
questions.explanation: Enlightenment writers such as Rousseau argued that sovereignty belongs to the people, an idea the French revolutionaries put into practice.

questions.stem: A major result of the French Revolution and Napoleon's wars was
options: the lasting return of feudal privileges across all of Europe
a decline in the power of the middle classes
the spread of nationalism and legal equality across Europe
the end of all monarchies in Europe by the year 1815
questions.explanation: French armies and the Napoleonic Code spread legal equality and abolished feudal dues, and resistance to French rule stirred nationalism in Spain, Germany and elsewhere. Many monarchies returned in 1815.

questions.stem: Which group would most likely have opposed the pamphlet's argument?
options: Merchants in Paris
Lawyers in the provincial towns of France
Peasants who paid heavy taxes
Nobles who held offices by birth
questions.explanation: The pamphlet attacks the privileges of nobles and clergy, who would lose their tax exemptions and offices. Merchants, peasants and lawyers were part of the third estate.

questions.stem: The speech is an example of
options: nationalism
mercantilism
absolutism
feudalism
questions.explanation: The speaker defines the nation by shared language and history and calls for one German state, the core of nineteenth-century nationalism.

questions.stem: How was the goal of the speech finally achieved?
options: An elected parliament united Germany in 1848
Austria united Germany under its emperor
France united the German states after 1815
Prussia united Germany through wars by 1871
questions.explanation: The liberal Frankfurt Parliament of 1848 failed; Germany was united under Prussian leadership after wars with Denmark, Austria and France, and the empire was declared in 1871.

questions.stem: Which movement of the 1800s was most similar to the one in the speech?
options: The Opium Wars
The partition of Africa by Europe
The Taiping Rebellion
The unification of Italy
questions.explanation: Italian nationalists also sought to join many states into one nation, which was largely done by 1861 and completed in 1870.

questions.stem: Nationalist ideas like those in the speech also challenged which kind of state in the 1800s?
options: Small states with a single national language
Island states such as Britain and Japan with long-settled borders
Empires ruling many peoples, such as Austria
City-states in East Africa
questions.explanation: Multiethnic empires such as Austria-Hungary and the Ottoman Empire faced nationalist movements among Serbs, Greeks, Czechs, Hungarians and others.

questions.stem: The pamphlet is an example of
options: a campaign to end slavery
an appeal for free trade with China
a defense of the plantation system
a call for war with France
questions.explanation: The pamphlet urges Parliament to end slavery in the British West Indies and asks families to boycott slave-grown sugar.

questions.stem: What happened to slavery in the British Empire after the pamphlet was written?
options: It spread to Britain itself
It was replaced by serfdom
It lasted in the West Indies until 1900
Parliament abolished it in the 1830s
questions.explanation: Parliament passed the Slavery Abolition Act in 1833, ending slavery in most British colonies, though it first imposed a period of forced apprenticeship.

questions.stem: Which reform in the 1860s was most similar in purpose to the one the pamphlet demands?
options: The Meiji government's new land tax
The opening of the Suez Canal
The emancipation of the serfs in Russia
The British Crown's takeover of India in 1858
questions.explanation: Russia freed its serfs in 1861, ending a form of unfree labor, though peasants had to pay for land. The other events had different purposes.

questions.stem: Adam Smith's The Wealth of Nations (1776) argued that
options: colonies should be ruled for profit by joint-stock companies
workers should seize the factories
states should control all trade through monopolies
free markets and the division of labor create wealth
questions.explanation: Smith argued against mercantilist monopolies and for free markets, in which the division of labor and competition increase a nation's wealth.

questions.stem: The second industrial revolution of the late 1800s is best known for
options: the first printing presses
steel, electricity and chemicals
the invention of the caravel and astrolabe
water-powered cotton mills
questions.explanation: After about 1870, new industries in steel, electricity, chemicals and later oil grew, led by Germany and the United States as well as Britain.

questions.stem: Railways and steamships in the 1800s most directly
options: slowed migration from Europe to the Americas sharply
cut the cost and time of moving goods and people
ended trade between Europe and Asia
raised the cost of shipping grain by sea
questions.explanation: Railways and steamships moved goods and people faster and cheaper over land and sea, which fed trade, migration and empire.

questions.stem: The letter best illustrates
options: a colony ruled through local kings
settler colonialism that took Indigenous land
a trading-post empire that left land in local hands
a treaty that protected every acre of Maori land in full
questions.explanation: In New Zealand, as in Australia and parts of Africa, growing numbers of European settlers took land from the Indigenous people, often by war after treaties were broken.

questions.stem: The process described in the letter was most similar to events in the same century in
options: Australia, where settlers took Aboriginal land
Japan, where foreigners were confined to ports
the Ottoman Empire, where Christians governed Istanbul
China, where the Qing kept its borders closed
questions.explanation: In Australia, British settlement also pushed Aboriginal peoples off their land as settler numbers grew.

questions.stem: The settler's last sentence is best used as evidence of
options: Maori military superiority in the long run
a British plan to withdraw its troops from New Zealand
an expectation that settlers would win
a shortage of settlers in New Zealand
questions.explanation: The settler admits the Maori forts are strong but expects growing numbers and guns to prevail, which is what happened in the wars of the 1860s.

questions.stem: The letter's account of the conflict is limited mainly because the writer
options: wrote centuries after the events took place
is a settler hoping to gain land
had never been to New Zealand
was a Maori chief
questions.explanation: A settler writing home sees the war from the side that wanted the land; Maori accounts would explain why the chiefs refused to sell.

questions.stem: According to the letter, the writer left home mainly because of
options: a government order to settle Malaya
a personal invitation from the Malay sultan to settle
better wages abroad and poor harvests at home
religious persecution in China
questions.explanation: He cites wages three times higher and failing harvests, typical push and pull factors for Chinese migration in the 1800s.

questions.stem: The broker's role described in the letter shows that many migrants
options: arrived with enough money to buy land of their own
traveled at government expense
were paid in advance by the mine owners
began abroad in debt for the cost of their passage
questions.explanation: Brokers paid passage and took the cost from the migrant's wages, so many laborers began their time abroad in debt.

questions.stem: The writer's hope that his brother will join him reflects
options: chain migration that built overseas Chinese communities
the return of all migrants within a year
a government ban on Chinese emigration that was enforced
the end of migration from China after 1880
questions.explanation: Migrants drew relatives and neighbors from home villages, building large Chinese communities in Southeast Asia and elsewhere.

questions.stem: Which later development shows a reaction against migration like that in the letter?
options: Laws restricting Asian immigration to Australia
Rising remittances to Chinese villages
The spread of tin mining in Malaya
The growth of overseas Chinese trading networks in Asia
questions.explanation: Several settler states passed laws to keep out Asian migrants, including Australia's Immigration Restriction Act of 1901, the basis of the White Australia policy.

questions.stem: The relationship described in the report is an example of
options: a colony governed by a British viceroy
a socialist planned economy
a self-sufficient economy closed to foreign trade and capital
economic imperialism without direct colonial rule
questions.explanation: Argentina was independent, but British investment shaped its economy around exports of wheat and beef, a form of economic imperialism.

questions.stem: Which technology made the trade in the report possible?
options: The printing press with movable type
The cotton gin
The caravel
Refrigerated steamships
questions.explanation: Refrigerated ships from the late 1870s let Argentina send frozen, and later chilled, meat across the Atlantic.

questions.stem: The investor's claim that Argentina could not hope for better partners overlooks
options: the absence of railways in Argentina
Britain's refusal to buy Argentine wheat or beef
Argentina's dependence on foreign capital
Argentina's rapid industrialization
questions.explanation: An investor praises the arrangement, but reliance on British capital and on a few exports left Argentina exposed when prices fell.

questions.stem: Social Darwinism was used in the late 1800s to
options: promote scientific study of the Americas
justify imperialism as the rule of the fittest
argue for the abolition of empires
support equal rights and the vote for colonized peoples
questions.explanation: Social Darwinists misapplied ideas of natural selection to claim that some races or nations were fitter to rule others, a justification for empire.

questions.stem: Under the Congo Free State of the 1880s to 1908, the Belgian king
options: ruled through an elected Congolese parliament and courts
freed the Congo from European control
banned the rubber and ivory trades
forced Congolese to gather rubber under brutal rule
questions.explanation: Leopold II ran the Congo as his personal colony and forced people to gather rubber, with mass killing and maiming; an international outcry led Belgium to take it over in 1908.

questions.stem: The Zulu kingdom's war with Britain in 1879 shows that
options: African states could win battles yet lose wars
Britain lost all of its colonies in southern Africa by 1880
the Zulu used machine guns to defeat Britain
African states never resisted European expansion
questions.explanation: Zulu forces defeated a British column at Isandlwana in 1879, but Britain sent more troops and conquered the kingdom within months.

questions.stem: The arrangement for the Arab provinces described by the historian is known as
options: the Tanzimat
the devshirme system
the millet system
the mandate system
questions.explanation: The League of Nations gave Britain and France mandates to govern former Ottoman lands such as Iraq, Syria and Palestine.

questions.stem: The division described by the historian most directly contributed to
options: Arab resentment of European rule
French rule over Turkey
the restoration of the Ottoman sultan
the end of Arab nationalism
questions.explanation: Arab leaders who had fought the Ottomans expecting independence instead got British and French rule, fueling Arab nationalism.

questions.stem: The Turkish republic described by the historian is best known for
options: restoring the Ottoman sultanate
secular reforms separating religion and state
joining the Soviet Union
making Islamic law the law of the land in every province
questions.explanation: Under Mustafa Kemal Ataturk the republic abolished the sultanate and caliphate, adopted a Latin alphabet and Western-style law codes, and separated religion from the state.

questions.stem: The fate of the Ottoman Empire after 1918 was most similar to that of
options: Britain, which gained new territory
Austria-Hungary, which broke into new states
Japan, which won German colonies
the United States, which grew in power and wealth
questions.explanation: Austria-Hungary also collapsed at the end of the war and broke into national states such as Austria, Hungary and Czechoslovakia.

questions.stem: The pamphlet's mention of oil, rubber and tin suggests that Japan's expansion was driven partly by
options: the defeat of Germany in 1918
a wish to end trade in Asia
the need for raw materials
a plan to free Korea from foreign rule
questions.explanation: Japan lacked oil and many raw materials, and it sought them in Southeast Asia; the pamphlet frames that expansion as liberation.

questions.stem: The purpose of the pamphlet was most likely to
options: call for peace and trade with the Western powers
present expansion as the liberation of Asia
apologize for the invasion of China
urge Japan to give up its colonies
questions.explanation: Calling the empire a sphere of common prosperity framed conquest as freeing Asia from the West, though Japanese rule was often brutal.

questions.stem: Japan's goals in the pamphlet were most similar to those of
options: the League of Nations, which sought disarmament
the United States, which sought to free the Philippines from Spain
Nazi Germany, which sought land and resources in eastern Europe
Britain, which gave up its colonies in 1940
questions.explanation: Like Japan in Asia, Nazi Germany justified conquest in eastern Europe by claims of racial destiny and the need for land and resources.

questions.stem: Japan's earlier invasion of which country had already led to war in Asia before 1940?
options: Australia
India
the Philippines
China
questions.explanation: Japan seized Manchuria in 1931 and began a full-scale war with China in 1937, years before it attacked the United States and Britain in 1941.

questions.stem: The speaker's refusal to join either camp is an example of
options: NATO
the non-aligned movement
the Warsaw Pact of communist states
the mandate system
questions.explanation: Newly independent states such as India, Indonesia and Egypt refused to join either Cold War bloc; the 1955 Bandung conference helped launch the non-aligned movement.

questions.stem: The two camps the speaker refers to were led by
options: the United States and the Soviet Union
Germany and Italy after 1945
Britain and France
China and Japan in East Asia
questions.explanation: In the Cold War, the United States led the capitalist bloc and the Soviet Union the communist bloc.

questions.stem: Despite speeches like this one, many newly independent states
options: joined the Soviet Union as new member republics
avoided all conflict during the Cold War
became sites of proxy wars
were never offered aid by either side
questions.explanation: The superpowers backed rival sides in places such as Korea, Vietnam, Angola and Afghanistan, turning local conflicts into proxy wars.

questions.stem: The speaker's experience of colonial rule helps explain the speech's emphasis on
options: joining a European alliance
restoring the old empires of Europe in Asia
avoiding a new foreign master
ending trade with neighbors
questions.explanation: Leaders who had just won freedom were wary that alliance with a superpower would bring a new master, which is why the speaker refuses both camps.

questions.stem: The campaign described in the report was led by
options: the World Health Organization and many governments
a single private company
the European Union working alone in Africa and Asia
the League of Nations
questions.explanation: The World Health Organization coordinated the smallpox eradication program from 1967, and the disease was declared eradicated in 1980.

questions.stem: The report is best used as evidence that
options: smallpox was still common in 1980
global cooperation could work even during the Cold War
the Cold War stopped all scientific exchange between the blocs
vaccines had no role in ending smallpox
questions.explanation: The officer credits teams in every country and both Cold War blocs working together, which is how eradication was achieved.

questions.stem: Which later disease showed the limits of the approach described in the report?
options: Polio, which was never treated with a vaccine
Smallpox, which returned in the 1990s
HIV/AIDS, for which no vaccine was found
The bubonic plague, which ended in 1347
questions.explanation: HIV/AIDS, identified in the early 1980s, spread worldwide and had no vaccine; treatment with drugs came later and unevenly.

questions.stem: Which later agreement showed the same kind of global cooperation on an environmental problem?
options: The Berlin Conference
The Montreal Protocol on the ozone layer
The Treaty of Versailles that ended the First World War
The Warsaw Pact
questions.explanation: In 1987 nearly every state agreed in the Montreal Protocol to phase out the chemicals that were thinning the ozone layer, a rare case of near-universal cooperation.

questions.stem: The Mexican Revolution that began in 1910 is best known for
options: creating a communist one-party state like the Soviet Union
restoring Spanish rule over Mexico
ending the Catholic religion in Mexico
demands for land reform from peasants
questions.explanation: Peasant leaders such as Emiliano Zapata demanded land, and the 1917 constitution promised land reform and limits on foreign ownership.

questions.stem: The Iranian Revolution of 1979 replaced the shah with
options: an Islamic republic led by Shia clerics
a communist government allied with Moscow
a military government backed by the United States
a restored Safavid dynasty
questions.explanation: Mass protests forced out the shah, and Ayatollah Khomeini led the creation of an Islamic republic governed by Shia clerics.

questions.stem: The genocide in Rwanda in 1994 grew in part from
options: a war between Rwanda and the Soviet Union in the 1980s
the end of apartheid in Rwanda
ethnic divisions hardened by colonial rule
the partition of India
questions.explanation: Belgian rulers had sharpened the line between Hutu and Tutsi with identity cards and favor to one group; in 1994 Hutu extremists killed hundreds of thousands of Tutsi and moderate Hutu.

questions.stem: Vietnam's Doi Moi reforms, begun in 1986, changed the country by
options: opening its economy to markets
making it a multiparty democracy with free elections
restoring rule by the French
ending all trade with its neighbors
questions.explanation: After years of a planned economy, Vietnam let farmers and businesses sell for profit and welcomed foreign investment, but the Communist Party kept one-party rule.
